title: MedlinePlus: Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure in Pregnancy
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM / NIH)
section_heading: Preeclampsia - Diagnostic Definition and Severe Clinical Signs
content: Preeclampsia is a serious multi-system gestational disorder characterized by new-onset hypertension (systolic BP >= 140 mmHg or diastolic BP >= 90 mmHg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) occurring after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive woman, combined with proteinuria (>= 300 mg per 24-hour urine collection or spot UACR >= 30 mg/mmol). In the absence of proteinuria, preeclampsia is diagnosed if hypertension occurs alongside thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 100,000/uL), renal insufficiency (serum creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL), impaired liver function (transaminases twice normal), pulmonary edema, or new-onset persistent severe headache and visual disturbances. Eclampsia is the occurrence of generalized seizures in a patient with preeclampsia.

title: MedlinePlus: Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure in Pregnancy
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM / NIH)
content: Definitive management of preeclampsia is delivery of the fetus and placenta. In women with high baseline risk factors (prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, pre-existing diabetes, multifetal gestation, or renal disease), daily low-dose aspirin (75-150 mg) initiated from 12 weeks of gestation until delivery significantly reduces the incidence of preeclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction. Severe acute hypertension (SBP >= 160 mmHg or DBP >= 110 mmHg) requires emergent antihypertensive therapy with intravenous Labetalol, oral Nifedipine, or intravenous Hydralazine to prevent maternal intracranial hemorrhage. Intravenous Magnesium sulfate is the agent of choice for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia and treatment of eclamptic seizures.
